explanations.explanation: Water it is, friend. Ezekiel, the prophet, sees it flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east (Ezekiel 47:1). It comes from under the temple itself. I think he stopped and stared, and I would have stopped right along with him.

I get the guess, since smoke is something I know plenty about from my ovens. But Ezekiel says he saw water flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east. No smoke at all. If a batch of mine came out looking like that, I'd be a very happy stamper.

Fire would sure get your attention, friend. But Ezekiel says what he sees is water flowing from under the threshold, toward the east. I'll keep the fire in my ovens where it belongs. This vision has a different thing going on.

That's a fair thought, but the text says something different. Out at the outer gate facing east, Ezekiel sees the water trickling out from the south side (Ezekiel 47:2). A trickle, friend, not a rushing stream. Hold onto that detail, because it's about to matter.

That's right. At the outer gate facing east, Ezekiel sees the water trickling out from the south side (Ezekiel 47:2). It's small out there. I'd have walked right past it with my mustache full of cookie boxes, and that's exactly why you keep watching.
Yes, ankle-deep. The man measures off a thousand cubits and leads Ezekiel through ankle-deep water (Ezekiel 47:3). That's still a small start. You could get your socks wet and call it a day.

That's quite a jump, friend. After the first thousand cubits, the text says the man led Ezekiel through ankle-deep water (Ezekiel 47:3). The water rises step by step, so chest-deep isn't one of the steps. It builds slowly.

Whoa, slow down, friend. After the first thousand cubits it's only ankle-deep (Ezekiel 47:3). Nobody's neck is getting wet yet. This water rises one measured stretch at a time, and Ezekiel gets to walk through every one of them.

Waist is right. The man measures another thousand cubits and Ezekiel is in knee-deep water. Then he measures again and leads him through waist-deep water (Ezekiel 47:4). Ankle, knee, waist, and every thousand cubits the water gets deeper.

Shoulders is a little too far up, friend. The text says the third stretch is waist-deep water (Ezekiel 47:4). Shoulders would be a different story altogether. This river is climbing, but one step at a time.

Chin-deep is quite a leap, friend. After the knees, the next stretch is waist-deep water (Ezekiel 47:4). Ezekiel's chin stays dry for now. I'd be glad about that if I were him, and I'd be gladder if I were a stamper.

True. After one more thousand cubits, the text says it was a river Ezekiel could not cross, because the water had risen and was deep enough for swimming. It was "a river that could not be crossed on foot." (Ezekiel 47:5) Remember where it started, friend: a trickle at the temple.

Not quite, friend. The text says that after one more thousand cubits, the water had risen and was deep enough for swimming. It was "a river that could not be crossed on foot." (Ezekiel 47:5) So Ezekiel isn't wading across this one. It's grown a lot since the trickle.
Yes, trees. When Ezekiel arrives back at the bank, he sees a great number of trees along both banks of the river (Ezekiel 47:7). Trees on both sides, friend. That's a lot of shade for one river.

Tents make sense for a riverbank, but that's not what Ezekiel sees. The text says that when he arrived, he saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river (Ezekiel 47:7). Nobody's camping here yet. It's a riverbank full of trees.

That's a big image, friend, but the text has a different one. Ezekiel says that when he arrived, he saw a great number of trees along both banks of the river (Ezekiel 47:7). No walls. Just trees lined up on both sides, like the river brought its own crowd.

Fresh, that's right. The man says the river flows into the Arabah, and when it empties into the Dead Sea, the water there becomes fresh (Ezekiel 47:8). The Dead Sea is the last place you'd expect a change like that. Yet the river just keeps going and gets the job done.

I see why you'd think so, since the Dead Sea doesn't sound like a lively spot. But the man says that when the river empties into it, the water there becomes fresh (Ezekiel 47:8). The river doesn't take anything away from it. It brings something new.

That's a dramatic guess, friend, but the text goes another way. The man says that when the river empties into the Dead Sea, the water there becomes fresh (Ezekiel 47:8). Fresh water coming in, and that's good news. No blood anywhere in this vision.
True. The man says, "…wherever the river flows, everything will flourish." (Ezekiel 47:9) Wherever it flows, friend. That's a river with a big job, and it does it everywhere it goes.
Not quite, friend. The man says, "…wherever the river flows, everything will flourish." (Ezekiel 47:9) So it's the opposite of withering or fading. Everywhere that river goes, things flourish.

That's right, fish of many kinds. The man says fishermen will spread their nets from En-gedi to En-eglaim to catch fish of many kinds, "like the fish of the Great Sea." (Ezekiel 47:10) Many kinds of fish, friend. I'm picturing a very full net and a very happy fisherman.

One kind sounds pretty modest, friend. The man says the fishermen will catch "fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea." (Ezekiel 47:10) So the nets pull in a whole variety. Think big on this one.

Two is a start, but this river is overachieving. The man says the fishermen will catch "fish of many kinds, like the fish of the Great Sea." (Ezekiel 47:10) That's a lot more than a pair. I'd say the fishermen are going to need bigger buckets.

Salt is right. The man says the swamps and marshes will not become fresh, and "they will be left for salt." (Ezekiel 47:11) Even with everything flourishing, the man says that about those spots. I'll just tell you what he said and leave the rest alone.

Grazing makes sense for open land, friend, but that's not what the man says. He says the swamps and marshes will not become fresh, and "they will be left for salt." (Ezekiel 47:11) No animals out there nibbling. Just salt.

Good thought for a place with water, friend, but the man says something else. The swamps and marshes will not become fresh, and "they will be left for salt." (Ezekiel 47:11) Salt, not crops. That's what he says, and I'm not adding anything to it.

I can see why that might sound right, since leaves wither all the time. But the man says the opposite: "Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail." (Ezekiel 47:12) These trees are on a different schedule. Their leaves stay put.
That's right, it's false. The man says, "Their leaves will not wither, and their fruit will not fail." (Ezekiel 47:12) No withering at all, friend. Compare that to my apron after one batch of dough.

explanations.answer: The water from the sanctuary flows to them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the man gives. Each month the trees will bear fruit, "because the water from the sanctuary flows to them." (Ezekiel 47:12) The water starts at the temple and flows out to them. That's where the fruit comes from.

explanations.answer: The fishermen carry water up to them
explanations.explanation: Fishermen hauling buckets would be a lot of work, friend. But the man never says that. He says the trees bear fruit each month "because the water from the sanctuary flows to them." (Ezekiel 47:12) The river does the watering, so the fishermen can just fish.

explanations.answer: The rain falls on them all year long
explanations.explanation: Rain all year would be a soggy kind of answer, friend. The man gives a different reason: the trees bear fruit each month "because the water from the sanctuary flows to them." (Ezekiel 47:12) It's the river that does the work.
Yes, healing. The man says, "Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing." (Ezekiel 47:12) Food from the fruit, healing from the leaves. Those trees are giving on both ends.

Weaving is a good use for leaves, friend, but it's not what the man says. He says, "Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing." (Ezekiel 47:12) So the leaves are for healing, not for making baskets. Nobody's setting up a loom by the river.

A leafy roof would be cozy, friend, but that's not the plan here. The man says, "Their fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing." (Ezekiel 47:12) Healing is what the leaves are for. You'd have to keep the roof over your head some other way.
